At a conference call today announcing third-quarter 2026 results, Apple said it is preparing for a tougher September quarter, with its most important products facing increasing supply pressures. Details below.

iPad, iPhone, and Mac to face growing supply constraints

Apple today announced strong third-quarter 2026 results, driven by double-digit revenue growth from iPhone and Mac, along with a 27% increase in profit.

However, Apple's iPad revenue declined 5% year-over-year, while the services business recorded its first quarter-over-quarter decline since 2022, with revenue of US$30.73 billion, up 12% year-over-year.

Wall Street's immediate reaction to Apple's results was far from positive, with the stock currently trading around 6.5% below its closing price.

On the conference call, Apple provided guidance for the September quarter and clearly pointed to challenges ahead, warning that supply constraints will significantly intensify and foreign exchange headwinds will persist.

Apple's CFO Kevan Parekh said that currency fluctuations alone are expected to reduce Apple's revenue growth next quarter by approximately 2.5 percentage points (compared to the June quarter), adding that "the impact of supply constraints is expected to increase significantly quarter-over-quarter."

Parekh listed iPhone, Mac, and iPad as products that will be significantly affected by supply constraints, and added:

On iPhone, we expect to continue seeing strong levels of market demand. However, we do expect iPhone revenue to be impacted by these foreign exchange headwinds and supply constraints. As a result, we expect iPhone's reported growth rate in the September quarter to reach a mid-teens percentage year-over-year. On services, we expect the September quarter's reported year-over-year growth rate to be roughly similar to the June quarter, except for the approximately 2.5 percentage point negative sequential impact from foreign exchange just mentioned.

He said Apple expects total revenue in the fourth quarter of 2026 to grow 9% to 11% year-over-year, with gross margins between 47% and 48%, assuming that "global tariff rates, policies, and their implementation remain unchanged as of this conference call, and that the global macroeconomic outlook does not deteriorate further from today."
